en: On the lofty mansion, a certain Supreme Being, sporting with his beloved upon the high terrace, fell asleep as Śrī does upon the coils of Śeṣa;
yet such is the wondrous course of fate that, on the banks of the Kampā in Kāñcī adorned by the Daughter of the Mountain, he was awakened by her while she was not by his side.

O fortunate one, the blue-haired goddesses, flying in celestial chariots from the city of Varuṇa, brought you here to see the God as he lay there in playful repose; yet, filled with apprehension at the words of the Goddess’s attendants, they released you not far from here. Then, in the sky, he heard a voice speaking thus regarding the gathering of the birds: *Kok_1.2*
If you were to dwell for five months in this field that shatters all calamities, then beyond that time, you would have no more pain from separation from beloved ones.
Having heard this again, he accordingly made his residence there; for even great affliction is highly regarded and praised if its future result is glorious.
There, having somehow endured two or three months—exceedingly long due to his separation from his beloved companions—this man, afflicted by passion, alas, alas!
beheld at the onset of Caitra a cuckoo, delightful with sidelong glances of the burgeoning beauty of spring and eager to taste the first buds of the mango tree. (Kok 1.4)

Approaching somewhat near him as he warbled with a sweet and melodious fifth-note melody, he—overwhelmed by the memory of his beloved’s voice—offered a libation of tears from the hollows of his cupped hands; then, finding some measure of relief, he clearly delivered this message in a distinct voice: *kokilakokilakūjitabhaṅgīmanoharamanoharavallabhāyām / māmakamānasamānavimarde mārutamārutamārutamāhuḥ // 1.6 //* "O cuckoo, they say that your wind-like song, charming with its melodic variations, is like the very breath of my beloved, who is so captivating and capable of crushing my heart. *śrāvaṇaśrāvaṇasampadupetāṃ tāṃ prati tāṃ prati tāmyasi kim tvam / māṃ prati māṃ prati yātu tavaiṣā vāsanā vāsanāvanitāyāḥ // 1.7 //* "Why do you languish for her, who is endowed with such excellence of hearing? Let this desire of yours go toward me, for I am the dwelling-place of that woman. *śrīharṣaṃ kavirājarājimukuṭālaṃkārahīraḥ sutaṃ śrīhīraḥ suṣuve jitendriyacayaṃ māmalladevī ca yam / ṣaṣṭhaḥ stabaka eṣa tasya kṛtau kāvyetarāyāṃ sphuṭaṃ niryātaḥ paripūrṇatāṃ rasabhṛtaḥ sadbhāvabhavyātmanaḥ // 1.8 //* This sixth canto has clearly reached completion in this work, which is other than a mere poem, composed by Śrī Hīra—who is the diamond ornament upon the crowns of the assembly of king-poets—and his wife Māmalladevī, whose soul is noble through true devotion and who has conquered the senses. *iti śrīmadāndhramahājanapadalalāmabhūte śrīmati kuvalayāpīḍapuraparisare mahati mahānagare sphīte śrīmatkolāhalanāmni sakalakalākalāpavidagdhasya paramavaidheyaśekharasya śrīmato rājaputrasya kumārasya krīḍāparvatopatyakāvanāvalīmaṇḍaleṣu viharataḥ śrīharṣasya kaveḥ kṛtiḥ śrīnaiṣadhīyacarite mahākāvye ṣaṣṭhaḥ sargaḥ //* Thus ends the sixth canto in the great epic poem *The Deeds of Nala*, the glorious composition of the poet Śrī Harṣa, who sports in the forest groves on the slopes of the pleasure-mountain of the illustrious prince Kumāra—the crest-jewel of the utterly simple-minded and master of all arts—residing in the great city named Kolāhala, a jewel of the beautiful Andhra country. *// samāptaṃ cedaṃ naiṣadhīyacaritaṃ mahākāvyam //* And thus the great epic poem *The Deeds of Nala* is finished.The provided text consists entirely of the character "a" repeated many times. Come here, dear friend; welcome indeed! Behold at your side the mango creeper, dripping with sweat-like sweet nectar from its newly blossomed flowers.
O fortunate one, this restless lady, whose eyes are like hovering bees, full of passion and beckoning with her trembling shoots, surely longs for your company.
Ah, I know you to be the foremost warrior of King Pañcabāṇa; you spread inner joy within me.
O friend of the cuckoo, under the pretext of your warbling, you teach what is beneficial: indeed, with your sweet songs, you unite amorous women who are full of pride with their beloveds. (Kok 1.7)
O cuckoo, do not make me, who am separated from my beloved, talkative; for generally, words of affection from those like me reach those like you.
Alas, by not seeing the kokila bird slightly hidden within its bud of young leaves, you, with your agitated soul, come to know the torment of those separated from their lovers.

O Lord of the great winged creatures, I fear that for as long as my tongue falters in hesitation to employ you in the task of one who desires to see the deer-eyed maiden, for that long your own heart will fall into exhaustion— you who are the opposite of one who procrastinates when it comes to fulfilling the requests of the distressed and the humble.

O Lord of Birds, carry my message and accomplish your brother’s duty; console my beloved with kind words, for she is afflicted by grief. For women tormented by separation, news of their beloved brought by a friend generally serves as some means of sustaining their lives. (Kok 1.10)
Victorious in the conquest of the three heavens, you must go to that land which has attained fame as Prāgjyotiṣa, the site of ancient austerities;
it lies beyond the Cūrṇī river in Kerala, cooled by the nectar of the glances of Lakṣmī as she gazes upon Govinda resting upon its shores. (Kok 1.11)
There you will surely see this young woman, who adorns the crest of the entire circle of women, now distressed by separation from me;
how indeed could that auspicious girl, whose limbs are as tender as a sprout of a golden plantain tree, endure the fire of passion which is like a bed of chaff?
I shall point out to you a path that is beneficial for you to travel without fatigue— a route where the heat is stilled on all sides by trees with lush shade—
where, O lord of birds, you will surely find those great monarchs who, though possessed of immense power, sport like fresh gardens.
Having witnessed the festival called Phālguna for Śrī Kāmākṣī, which is attended by the gods, those women of sweet speech— mounted upon various celestial chariots as they return to their own abodes—
are accompanied by you, O Varuṇanagarī, their voices made tremulous by the desire to hear your conversation as far as the shore of the western ocean.

Carrying offerings of the fragrance of fresh creepers and flowers, sprinkling cool, gentle droplets all along the path, and speaking most sweetly with the humming of bees, these favorable winds from the groves on the trembling banks turn toward you as kinsmen. (Kok 1.15)
O dear friend, salute from afar this holy aerial chariot on the slope of the Karigiri mountain, belonging here to Śauri, the lord of Kāñcī, so that you may see him again.
Even today, the pigeons nesting in its golden roof-ridges mistake the smoke rising from the sacrifices of Brahmā for the lingering smoke of his own sacrificial fires.
Among the eighteen sacred seats (pīṭhas), you should worship the honored Kāmapīṭha, where the Supreme Goddess herself is present beyond all trembling.

Upon reaching her, whose cloud-like eyes are accompanied by the bow of her eyebrows, the land of Tuṇḍīra flourishes with the harvest of easily obtained poetic inspiration through the rain of her compassion. 1.17.
Fly up from this Bakula grove and, proceeding clockwise around the garden grounds, go to the holy Single Mango Tree (*ekāmravṛkṣa*);
at its base, which is naturally beautiful, dwells in person the moon-crested God known as Valayāṅka, who has abandoned all desire for Kailāsa.

Upon seeing you suddenly ascending through the path of the sky, O Śambhu, young bees will rise from the creepers— fanned by the wind from the pair of your wings— as their bodies are drenched with nectar, imitating the casting of moist side-glances sent by the beauty of the garden.
O cuckoo, while you are soaring toward the edge of the sky, the land of Kāñcī—adorning the earth with its unique dignity—is clearly visible to you.

Since your heart has been captivated by its beauty, do not delay in departing; for those like you, there is no higher station than that which is attained through the protection of one's kin. (Kok 1.20)

Taking refuge in hope, which is marked by the weapon of the noose, you—possessing great speed—will see before you the Ocean of Milk. Its waves are stirred by chowries in the form of *kramuka* and *kuvalaya* trees growing upon its shores; it is frequented by young female bees, intoxicated from drinking the honey-sweet nectar of blooming lotuses.

With its expansive expanse pervaded by the intensely spreading shadows cast by your wings—dark as the neck of the Bird-vanquisher of Cities (Śiva)—you clearly delineate the path of your journey through the sky, manifesting the beauty of the Yamunā’s braid as it meets the Sindhu out of affection for the river. 1.22.
Seeing you together with each mango tree and its flower buds, as the slender-limbed women strike the young *aśoka* trees with their reddish feet,
the boundaries of the groves on the riverbanks will surely resound on all sides with the charming tinkling of their anklets.

O friend, having emerged from the bath with the jars of their breasts beautiful with droplets of water, adorned with auspicious ornaments touched by dark mud and pure fragrances—having seen those lovely Dravidian beauties on her bank, your delay will likely last for a moment. 1.24.

Thereafter, you should behold those agrahāras situated to the south of the river, whose surrounding trees are grey with the masses of smoke produced by the sacrificial offerings, whose monasteries resound with the mature and praiseworthy Vedic chants that purify all, and whose expanses are enclosed by tanks sanctified by the ritual baths of the most excellent brahmins.

That erudition in the Vedas, that immersion in all the sciences, and that stainless poetry with its unfading and flowing sweetness—if one were to recite all this here, the parrots dwelling there would make it manifest on every branch of the trees surrounding their homes. (Kok 1.26)

Passing beyond them, O friend, enter the temple of Paśupati at Vilvakṣetra— invited as it were by the breezes from the courtyard that stir the tips of the banner-cloths— and make fruitful the eyes of the Cola women, who, with necks upraised, gaze upon you with lashes like a row of blossoming blue lotuses.
It is said that Kāma became a moth before the sparks of her eyes; but from the glance of the Moon-crested Lord, the destroyer of worldly existence, he cried out, "Do not fear!
She, dark in complexion, sweet in speech, and flickering in the play of her glances, shines upon his left lap, milking out every desire through her extraordinary compassion.

There, O friend, the groves—with birds uttering welcoming cries sweet with intense intoxication, scattering offerings of flowers and honey, and fanning you with their sprouts—will honor you, the minister of the Fragrant One; for people treat one who shares their king’s affection just as they do the king himself.
At that time, at the conclusion of their dalliance, the beautiful women in turn will emerge from the thick bowers of creepers with their lower garments slipping from their hands;
as you wander there, they—free from perspiration by the breezes from your wings—will honor you with sidelong glances that move with languid, weary archings of the brows.
Proceeding further, having crossed this country, you should behold the forests of the Colas, where the eyes of restless-eyed does are darkened by the plumage of peacocks;
where the thickets are filled with beds of blossoming jasmine and clusters of guñjā berries; and where, in every bower, the amorous dalliances of Śabara couples are made manifest.

There, the winds— vomiting forth sprays of cool water from flower buds, stumbling through dense groves amidst the mists of mountain torrents, and cherished by forest deities sporting on vine-swinging cradles— will serve you with their burden of flickering yak-tail fans.

Kissing a fresh sprout like a bimba-fruit lip, and having attained an embrace upon a fresh bud like a breast, you shall enjoy the mango creepers there at your pleasure; for when the passion of the forest has blossomed, what man would wish to abandon them? (1.33)

And having pecked with their beaks at the golden-brown clusters from the mango grove, O dear friend, the peacocks— perceiving you as a fresh rain-cloud accompanied by lightning as you rise up, streaking the expanse of the sky with the variegated shadows of your wings— will dance playfully, the weight of their tail-feathers swaying.
Not far from that [mountain] is visible the Kāverī, a flood of rut-fluid from the Sahya-elephant, upon which royal swans have descended in a multitude;
in the midst of her, like an emerald set in the pearl-string of the earth’s necklace, Raṅganātha is seen, dark as a cloud, reclining upon the serpent Śeṣa. (Kok 1.35)
O Lord of Cuckoos, entering the Hosalas— fragrant with the blossoms of garden trees and surrounded by cities, market towns, and villages on the banks of the Puṇyānā river—
reach the dwelling known as Lakṣmīnārāyaṇapura within the heart of Murāri, and become the foremost among the purifiers.

There, even the god of love becomes helpless before the amorous charms of the courtesans—women whose lovely hair is adorned with fragrant flowers, whose bodices burst open from the slopes of their breasts swelling with the heat of youth, and whose gentle smiles mingle with the rays of pearl ornaments upon their noses. (Kok 1.37)
O cuckoo, if those beloved women, their hearts bound by pride, should not honor their submissive lovers, then abandon your single cry of "kuhū.
Let there be for the young men, embraced by the vine-like arms of their own trembling wives, side-long glances accompanied by tender smiles directed toward you.
You should take refuge on the Sahya mountain, world-renowned for the sounds of the ornaments of sky-dwelling women as they sport within their resonant bowers of creepers;

for it is there that the Lord of the Bhṛgu clan, having personally desisted from the destruction of the Kṣatriyas and having entrusted the entire circle of the earth to the Brahmins, resides upon its slopes.

If you see from afar the fires fed by smoke, their masses of flames like matted hair, and the forest trees shimmering with clusters of shoots and frequented by hovering bees, you must infer the presence of water; for when one is in a perilous situation, hesitation brings about suffering, and prompt action is what saves one. (Kok 1.40)
Having seen there the temple of Amalaka on the earth where the wielder of the Śārṅga bow resides, descend from that mountain with your wings slightly folded;
then behold before you the flourishing land of Kerala, thick with betel-nut trees on the shore of the ocean, which was the site of the onset of the prowess of Bhṛgu’s son’s arms.
If you must attain one, then behold, O traveler on the banks of the Vāṅmayī, the Lord who has the moon as his crest-ornament, the fierce destroyer of Dakṣa’s sacrifice!
Not far from him dwells Bhadrakālī, who, standing upon the head of the lord of beasts, destroyed the wooden pillar with the tip of her sharp trident.
Sprinkled by clear droplets from mountain torrents, stay in the sky and honor him, appearing like a fresh black cloth covered with pearls.
If your attendants should drive you away under the mistaken impression that you are a crow, then utter a slight caw; surely one who is weary and distressed makes his presence known through his voice.

Having thus propitiated the Destroyer of Cities with devotion and obtained His grace, and being drawn on at every step by the side-long glances of the Kerala women, O friend, enter the capital city of the mountain-kings, which possesses blossoming gardens and high palaces that push upward the paths of the stars. 1.44.
In whose lineage was born the king named Hariścandra, and from whom originated the restoration of the Kaumārilas;
and in whose battles Caṇḍikā stands present for the destruction of enemies—for whose praises would not the mouth of anyone be purified? (1.45)
While wandering through that city, the beloved of Rukmiṇī will look upon you with glances full of affection, thinking, "He is a dear friend of my son.
You should dispel the fatigue of your journey by strolling somewhere in his very garden, where the flowers and sprouts have been gently plucked by young women.

If the princess named Svātī, her girdle tinkling with playful movements, should have come there with tender feet and palms placed in the hands of her companions to serve the Lord, then some instruction for your songs would surely arise from her spontaneous conversation, O cuckoo. (Kok 1.47)
As she approaches—her waist bent low, oppressed by the weight of her breasts; her face dappled with drops of perspiration;

and weary from the burden of her hips—you shall receive her sidelong glances, beautiful with the flickering movement of her darting pupils, as she sprinkles you with the nectar-drops from the slightly opened buds of her lips.
For a short time, her cluster of blossoms—its covering of fresh shoots withered and its beauty rejected by trembling young bees—was being consumed;
yet when you, O fortunate one, set out on your journey, she revealed her favor, shedding a few teardrops under the guise of trickling honey. (Kok 1.49)
O friend, although you must travel south for the sake of protecting my life, you should instead go toward the west;
for if you do not enjoy there the multitude of Śambhu’s riches—the grove of Dhūta—fanned by the breezes from the river at the edge of his crown, what is the use of a life lived?

Entering that magnificent palace of Dhūrjaṭi, which, with its lofty mansions washed in white plaster, seems to laugh at the Silver Mountain (Kailāsa), you shall experience for a moment the grace of a palm-leaf fan for those earthly gods who have grown weary from the constant performance of prostrations at every corner. 1.51.

Having emerged from the golden turrets where carved birds perch, bow down without hesitation to Śiva, with your limbs motionless in meditation, while you are gazed upon by the Daughter of the Mountain with pure glances held in secret curiosity, wondering, "Is this the reflection of my husband’s neck? (Kok 1.52)
O friend, look with reverence at the gods, such as Brahmā and Indra, who are bound in service by the mutual restraint of Śrī Nandin’s eyebrows;
and in another place, listen to the soft lute-sounds of the Kinnarīs singing, which are indistinguishable from your own warbling. (Kok 1.53)
You bestow divine sovereignty upon those who worship you, yet you wander about begging for alms; you carry Gaurī on your lap, yet you have reduced the five-arrowed god of love to ashes;
pervading the entire universe, you flash forth, yet you are sought after by the final words of the scriptures—O Ocean of Wonders, who is capable of defining your true nature?
Having praised thus, stay until the sun reaches the western mountain at the edge of the outer grove;
there you shall behold the immediate fruit of your eyes—the dance of the Moon-crested Lord, graced by the playful, sidelong glances of Gīrījā as she gracefully performs her lāsya dance.

At that time, I suspect that the splendor of the moon’s orb—marked with its distinct spot as it rises for a moment—enters, under the guise of its reflection, the heart of the beautiful women who enjoy the offerings of Bali; for that heart, held upon the slope of their breasts, is full of passion like a vessel. (Kok 1.56)
When the world has lost its light due to the darkness— which, like the mass of luster from the necks of Paśupati scattered in all directions, resembles the bees upon the blue lotuses of the sky—
rest for a while in some large cluster of tree branches and spend that night right there with your wings weary and drooping.
O cuckoo, at night the breezes from the shore of the western ocean, swaying the ripples and having their pearls drunk by the slightly blossoming water-lily buds in the lakes,
will serve you as you sleep soundly while stealing away the sprouts of perspiration born of lovemaking from the fair-browed women.

O friend, when the solar ray—resembling a forest fire on the first mountain peak at its rising, and as beautiful as a cluster of young *aśoka* blossoms—has appeared, you should set out once again at dawn; for those like you, the personal hardship endured in helping a friend leads only to happiness.
When your lover reaches your side at dawn from the edge of the lotus grove, he will surely behold you in the midst of it, overcome by the fever of passion for me;
and when I have gone far away, by the power of fate, as your friend grieves, you will certainly feel a doubled resolve to go, remembering me again and again.
Having seen the Lord Bālakṛṣṇa dwelling in the vicinity of Śambara, adorned with the friendship of Lopāmudrā, and about to grace the quarters of the sky,
go to where the great poets beginning with Śaṅkara— whose fame transcends all bounds— are celebrated as fragrant as the groves of Kolānīla.

Behold the ocean, the abode of Lakṣmī’s husband, the flower garden of Śiva, and the kitchen of all the winds; where it is seized by masses of winged mountain-kings as if they were suddenly emerging with speed, and by the fierce outspread of our arms upon the boats. 1.62.
With its white sandy banks strewn by garlands of waves and its shores lined with lush, flowering trees,
you travel from land to land, respectfully drunk in by the cupped eyes of lovely-eyed women whose faces are upturned in curiosity.
That city known as Kukkuṭakroḍa, which touches the sky with the tops of its palaces, will surely bring delight to your eyes;
there, the foremost of heroes and preeminent warriors—lords of mountains and oceans who have become tributary kings through the firmness of their own prowess—protect the realm.

In every house there was a palace washed with fresh lime; in every palace, a pleasure-couch was prepared with fragrant flowers; and upon every couch, a pair of lovers—woman and beloved—was overcome by passion. As he wandered from one couple to the next, he was indeed the Mind-born God, the hero of the universe.
A fresh water-lily on the ear is useless where there is a sidelong glance; a necklace is a burden upon breasts that shine with gentle smiles;
and where there is a thick mass of glossy hair, a flower for the sake of auspiciousness is redundant when there is already a fragrance like that of a young deer. (Kok 1.66)

Where, having learned that Lakṣmī had made her dwelling there, I believe the Lord of the Waters—his heart overwhelmed with affection—repeatedly presents a flotilla of ships filled with heaps of jewels brought from hundreds of other islands, as if embracing her with his waves. (Kok 1.67)
Do not begin to chew, with the notion that they are tender sprouts, the mass of light resembling thick vermilion on the tops of those palaces made of reddish stones;
for upon seeing you, the young women, with their lotus-eyes fixed at the windows, will laugh, clapping their hands as their breasts heave.
Having somehow withdrawn your gaze from that source of wonders, you should fly along the path, licking the honey of the flowers of the trees;
and as you go, you should steal the hearts of the doe-eyed women of the countryside with the sounds of your throat, which are like the war-trumpets of the army of Love. 1.69.
Having reached the radiant lights that have pacified the Kali age through the practice of Brahman, go to Śvetāraṇya, the highly esteemed abode of Mṛtyuñjaya;
a place which people, even upon seeing it but once from afar, will certainly never again behold the face of Death with its frown knit upon the forehead.
The lotus-foot of Śiva, which is to be served by the hand of the daughter of the mountain as she massages it, and which was kicked by the chest of the mace-wielder (Kārttikeya)—
that very foot, when stepped upon by the Lord of Mountains, caused the emperor of the Rākṣasas to cry out in pain, his face like a clod of earth and his forest of arms cast down.
Beside which flows the wave-filled river named Nīlā, like the Gaṅgā fallen from the head of Śiva during his whirling dance at twilight;
on its bank stands a certain dark-blue splendor, as dark as the petal of a blue lotus, beloved by the boat-pond and resting within the embrace of the arms of the Yamunā.
O dear friend of my beloved, who has come for the great service of Māgha, there the Keralī women meet gracefully with their lovers in a grove;
where, having drunk again and again the enchanting fragrance of their mouths, even now the young bees remain mostly intoxicated and do not smell the lotuses at all. (Kok 1.73)
During these days, the ocean—its lotuses covered by masses of *śaivāla* moss, its swans wandering upon the shifting sands—has been reduced to emaciation by the rays of the sun.
I imagine that my beloved wife, distressed by the state of separation, might follow after it, her dark tresses scattered like a mass of *ālaka* curls and her girdle slipping from her hips. (Kok 1.74)

If the Teacher, dwelling in the embrace of Śambara, should travel along the paths on its banks on a swift horse, eager for the hunt, you might wipe away his drops of perspiration with the gentle breeze of your wings; for service to lords at the proper time brings both pleasure and lightness.

The foremost of the twice-born in Kerala are renowned throughout the world as the most excellent; yet even among them, a certain greatness belongs to those who dwell in the middle region of Vallī and Kauṇi.
Furthermore, wherever the waters and breezes of this [river] spread, there the character, learning, and spiritual power of those people become preeminent.
The Guru has no authority over their praises; what then can be said of those who are inferior to us? O brother, listen further: there remains only a small portion of what was introduced.
Having crossed that river which flows with nectar, fly toward the lands purified by the multitude of virtues belonging to the Nārāyaṇa of the eyes, where clusters of *ākanda* trees abound.

That lotus-foot of Kātyāyanī—the slayer of Mahiṣa, whose abode is the City of Liberation—which was once held compassionately by Śambhu at the time of her marriage and somehow, with great care, placed upon the surface of a stone; that foot, tender as a young sprout, is now to be beheld. (Kok 1.78)
A short while before, you should visit the holy abode of the great sage, the family preceptor of the two Mīmāṃsā schools, on that famous battlefield.
There, whenever a multitude of scholars arrives with the intent to debate, the flock of parrots dwelling in the eaves of the lecture hall remains constantly present.

Whether it be the exposition of the scriptures, the stories of Hari and Hara, or conversation with the wise regarding hospitable rites for guests—if these should captivate his mind, then you, seated on the mountain in the pleasure grove surrounded by confident brahmins, should cry out; for he will surely be delighted upon hearing your sweet, well-spoken words.

O friend, if a wise man should behold you—composed in praiseworthy meters, employed for a beautiful purpose, audible through words graced by the essence of nectar-like flowers, and possessing unerring movement—as if you were slackened by the difficulty of reaching a distant goal, then surely your conduct is entirely pure. (Kok 1.81)
As you set out from his side, may the fragrant breezes— carrying the pure froth of the cud chewed by the bulls attached to the mouths of the Lord of Bulls,
white as kunda flowers, and scented by the tossing locks of Gaurī as she plays upon Śaṅkara’s lap— alleviate your distress as you approach the city of Vṛṣapura.

If the frontal portion [of Gaurī] is seen, bent by the weight of her breasts, with moving eyes, yet the rear portion, adorned with lovely tresses and hips, is not seen—thus the Blessed One, who possesses eight forms and desires to behold both simultaneously, bears a pair of bodies; he, the one to be served for the sake of liberation. (Kok 1.83)

In whose crown—the interior of the pavilion formed by the circle of the heads of the Creator (Brahmā)—the doubts of the gods of the earth who dwell upon the words of the Vedas are severed; [a crown] where the forehead and eyes are set ablaze by the breath-winds of the serpent-ornament, and which is empowered by the trickling drops of nectar from the perspiring moon.

Not far from there, having entered out of devotion to the golden palace, bow down to Girijā, who is the very embodiment of prosperity; for she is the Mother of the Universe, while the Guardians of the Quarters—whose purposes are fulfilled by the sidelong glances bestowed by Aṇimā standing at the edge of the doorway—crowd the outer courtyard as they wait upon her.
As you traverse the sky, plunging into the mass of blossoming *tāpiñcha* trees belonging to the Lord of Saṅgama-village with your spreading, body-like splendors resembling their dark hue,
I think that— recollecting the comfort of dwelling among rows of fresh *tamāla* trees due to their similar shade— you will not be perceived by the people as distinct from them for even a moment.
On your way, take refuge in Kālī’s abode, a great forest where the hosts of gods have come for eternal service;
there, when the sacrificial buffalo—intended as an offering—is seized by fierce spirits who tear at its horns with ropes, Vijayā, laughing aloud, restrains him as he cries out.
Behold before you the lovely city of Añjanakhala, protected by Śaṅkara, where the horses of the sun are fanned by the breezes from the cloths on palace banners;
there, the powder-scented breeze kisses the perspiring cheeks of beautiful young women, like a lover kissing the lotus-face of one exhausted by dalliance. (Kok 1.88)

And that river is to be beheld immediately thereafter, where, as the great splendor of the rising fragrance unfolds, the red lotuses— perfumed by the musk from the necks of the women of Mahodayapura who have bathed in its dark waters— are clearly perceived as attaining a likeness to a grove of blue water-lilies.

Beautiful, clear, with eyes like saphara fish, the splendor of breasts like ruddy geese, with eyebrows like waves, a face like a lotus, and lovely curls of hair—she is to be enjoyed by those who have descended into her favor, being full of passion and sweetness; for such is the path of those possessing profound depth, which is difficult for others to fathom. (Kok 1.90)
O fortunate one, when you are playfully suspended in the sky over a river, the Malaya breeze— seeing your reflection trembling in the water as clear as a broken jewel—
will coo sweetly again and again, mistaking it for a cluster of dark blue lotuses swaying in the force of the waves.
As you reach its southern shore at that very moment, there shall spread before your eyes a land of surpassing splendor;
know it as the destination that has eclipsed the majesty of the celestial city, renowned in every direction by the name of Jayantī.

O Ornament of Wisdom, that city of yours will likely be easy to find even without being pointed out, with its pleasure gardens where vine-thickets have been enjoyed by intoxicated women, its lakes where bees wander as if lost due to the agitation caused by sporting swans, and its gate-towers whose pinnacles are fashioned from rows of jewels.

The northern part [of the city], which he—the Cakravāka bird who is a bee to the lotus of the Vedas—indeed inhabits, is filled with incomparable networks of jewels that mark the birth and abiding of Lakṣmī; it contains within it mountains and possesses a praiseworthy growth manifested through the rising of its various arts.
Regarding this vast city as the supreme body of the ocean itself, he dwells there. (Kok 2.1)

"Look at the side of the moon; it bears a stainless resemblance to your face. Thus addressed by their lovers, O fair-faced one, the deer-eyed women on the palace rooftops, as if out of jealousy upon seeing the dark spot behind the moon, cast sidelong glances whose beauty surpasses that of blue lotuses. (Kok 2.2)
In every street, where the ground is paved with fragments of the stone that slew Balaripu, the masses of rays from your necklace—dark as a net of clouds—coalesce;
there, even when darkness has begun which cannot be dispelled even by the rays of the sun, the secret trysts of the tremulous-eyed women proceed without fear during the day.
On that night when the moon— its orb truly rubbed by the tips of the silken banners atop the palace towers due to its theft of the beauty of the lotus-faces of young women—
was seen by the world to bear a deep-set scar like a speck of collyrium, alas, the foolish folk said, "It is a red hare," and so on.
Where the rays of emerald light, tossed like young moss-creepers by the waves of the celestial river as they surge from the moon-chambers above,
begin to be chewed by the horses of the sun, who, wandering the long path of the sky, start to graze with flickering snouts under the mistaken impression that they are grass.
In that garden, where the clouds—indistinguishable from swarms of bees—cling to the treetops amidst clusters of bowers that darken the quarters of the sky;
there, at their own season, the waters in the ponds become exceedingly fragrant, intensified by the spreading radiance of crystal rays from the edges of the steps.

"O innocent one, did my lover eat before others in my jeweled chamber?"—to her who asks this, the friends, putting the newlywed bride to shame with their faint smiles, show her the peerless body of that woman reflected on the wall, covered in nail-marks. (Kok 2.7)
When the bow was strung with the creeper of her eyebrows, the stalk of sugarcane placed upon it assumed the role of an arrow; the lotus set near her eye likewise took on the nature of a shaft.
Even as the line of hair assumed the state of a bowstring for her bimba-like lips, the Lord of Love caused the swarm of bees to fall away.

Where, seeing that the garments of the lovely-eyed women had slipped—leaving their braids hanging down, their breasts trembling, and the knot of their lower robes loosened—the libertines embraced them; and at the conclusion of the elaborate display of their seduction, they roused once more the exhausted efforts of those with half-closed eyes toward the waves of passion. (Kok 2.9)
In this [rainy season], the clouds—resting upon the edges of palaces made of emerald slabs—would not be discernible if they did not emit a thunder that is pleasant to the ear;
and the lightning-creeper is just like the girdle slipping from the broad hips of a beloved woman as she moves during the fresh dalliance of love they have begun anew. (Kok 2.10)
In that city, to the right of the abode of Lakṣmī’s lover, stands the residence of my beloved, surrounded on all sides by jewel-palaces;
in its center is a mansion wrought of gold, which bears a multitude of projecting eaves, wherein the Goddess Śrī sports like a lotus upon a shimmering pericarp.

"Great fortune, the majesty of the arms of the Lord of Rati, a flood of auspiciousness through its redundancy, and here too the infinity of connoisseurs—it is for these reasons that the lords of poets praise the venerable abode of Māra, having formed his name by taking the first syllables of these words. (Kok 2.12)
There shines a charming pleasure-pool, its flight of stairs bordered by clusters of lotuses perpetually smiling with the radiance of rubies;
I imagine that mallikākṣa birds dwell there to practice their swimming, as my beloved approaches the clear water to bathe.
On its bank there is a grove, and therein stands a mango tree surrounded by young cuckoos like yourself, greedy to taste its sprouts;
and at its side is a charming mādhavī creeper bent down with clusters of blossoms—those two which I respectfully caused my beloved and me to ascend during our wedding ceremony. (Kok 2.14)
Not far from that [tree], on a surface of emerald, stands a certain campaka tree with its basin bound in gold, its root drenched by the weight of cool water.
Having obtained the rosy hue of your friend’s lotus-face, that fortunate one produces a flower whose color matches the creeper of her body. (Kok 2.15)

There, in that sandalwood grove where the palace peacocks dance in play having long abandoned their association with snakes, and where the thick shade wards off the rays of the sun, stands a jeweled bower of creepers upon a floor of gems; therein, indeed, our creeper of love constantly wound itself about in some indescribable way. 2.16.
Moreover, near that fawn-eyed woman stands a *kuravaka* tree, its trunk dripping with the sweet sap of its glossy branches and resounding with the humming of bees;
its body embraced at all times by her arms—which possess the graceful curve of an elephant’s trunk—it bears horripilation in the guise of its budding blossoms. (Kok 2.17)

If she were not seen sitting upon a flower-bed prepared by her attendants in any of these aforementioned places, then that palace of hers, which is most dear to her, would be some great sapphire; and there my beloved of lovely form would be visible like lightning within a cloud.
She is a pill of nectar for the eyes, the very essence of the Creator’s creation, the first bud of the moon of beauty, and the lamp of the earth-mother;
she is the golden banner-staff of Kāmadeva, the lord of the three worlds, and a digit of the moon for the ocean of erotic sentiment—she is my second life. (Kok 2.19)
Behold her, submerged within a circle of intense and exquisite beauty; how will you not recognize her in the midst of these other tremulous-eyed women?
Tell me, by what means is the lunar form made known to the world at night, when it bathes the universe in a web of moonlight in the presence of the stars?
The moon, free from blemish, is a mass of dense fragrance and darkness; the two golden mountains are a portion of the sky encircled by swarms of bees;
the lovely pair of lotuses are a soft pair of elephant trunks; and all this, fashioned by Madana, has come together, O gentle one, to become this [beautiful lady]. (Kok 2.21)
Her sidelong glances, languid and rolling, humble the pride of the deer; her brow, trembling with coquettish grace, robs the waves of all their arrogance;
her hands do not tolerate the majesty of the sprouts of the wish-fulfilling tree; and her speech maintains a youthful friendship with the fifth note of your [the cuckoo’s] song. (Kok 2.22)
If that beauty were gold, her face would be the moon; if that sweetness of her bimba-like lower lip were honey, it would turn bitter.
If her slender body were a *mālatī* vine, it would be like iron; if her thighs were the golden pillars of a plantain tree, they would be mere pretenses. (Kok 2.23)
Alas, as I describe her limbs—which possess a fresh essence of loveliness precisely as they were described before—the flow of my words continues.
When the mind is thus rendered helpless, what indeed can it do? Whatever the heart reflects upon, that very thing becomes the subject of speech.

Today, while I, her lover, am away from home due to the misfortune of fate, alas, as these days pass like entire aeons, that delicate-limbed woman will surely become distressed by the intense agony of separation; longing for me, she will grow weary like a peahen exhausted by the feverish heat of a swooning summer.

Whenever I, out of affection, would pluck a red lotus from the pond and place it upon her ear each day after parting her hair— hair adorned with the luster of her sidelong glances— at that moment, alas, the sprout-like hand of this girl, overwhelmed with anxiety, would surely rest against her cheek as an ornament reaching to the root of her ear.

O friend, those two whose eyelashes once trembled as they gazed upon me—when I was formerly driven far away by Fate, making them like trees stripped of leaves—now, their eyes, motionless due to the flooding of inner tears, bear the wretchedness of a lotus bristling with droplets of frost. (Kok 2.27)

That lower lip of hers, which was kissed by me with deep passion, skill, tenderness, longing, and thirst at the end of our union—and which, being repeatedly sprinkled with the nectar of her playful words and fragments of smiles, yet languishes under the hot breaths of my sighs—is exceedingly red. (Kok 2.28)
Surely her two breasts must be the two pleasure-mountains of King Madana, the city of his splendor, with their bases slightly pale;

I imagine that, fearing my separation, he has bestowed upon them another necklace of pearls resembling autumnal stars, in place of the string of pearls he is making them discard through the streams of her tears.
Although she has abandoned her attachment to ornaments, that girdle—which was woven by me with pearls gathered one by one—remains fastened upon her broad hips;
and because those delicate-limbed maidens have their great hips adorned by it, Love indeed considers his royal capital to be encompassed by a rampart of *sāla* trees.
The pair of her thighs, which serve as the reins for restraining the elephant known as my mind, have now become weary and utterly exhausted from the burden of her hips.
Alas, alas! While I was engaged in massaging them, constant and boundless delights were interrupted by various unforeseen obstacles. (Kok 2.31)
Her lotus-feet, resembling young shoots, were exhausted by the coming and going of her tremulous-eyed self as far as the doorway out of fear of my approach;
alas, they were repeatedly subjected to false stumbles in speech so that, in falling at my feet, she might receive beatings from me. (Kok 2.32)
Although the blazing fire of separation withers her vine-like body, it nevertheless doubles her splendor of beauty;
for while fire reduces a heated gold leaf to extreme thinness, it indeed produces a superior excellence of color.

Alas! She carries particles of dust upon her tresses, a flood of tears in her eyes, a cheek in her hand, a necklace of white lotus stalks upon her breast, and a soiled, rough silk garment upon her hips. Let this be; enough with these many lamentations—let there be no further delay. (Kok 2.34)
Having stayed at the mango tree first mentioned, and having bitten a sprout that has the luster of your beloved’s innocent lower lip at your leisure, you must then look for her.
She may be asking about the state of the Malaya breeze, or she may be inquiring with humility after my news; or else, she may be entreating you, saying, "Tell me the story of that hard-hearted one."

"Does the sandalwood paste, cool as snow-water, cause distress? Are the slow-moving breezes from the yak-tail fans perhaps not pleasant?"—to her friends asking this, even though her fever was extreme, she smiled and comforted their hearts by saying that everything was delightful. (Kok 2.36)

"The Malaya breezes are stirring; bar the lattice with its doors. Terrify the five-arrowed god, who hurls multitudes of arrows, by uttering the name of Śambhu. Release the cakora bird to roam in the moonlight. Thus she repeatedly instructed her maidservant, whose eyes were filled with tears. (Kok 2.37)

Whether she has reached the painted hall by the hands of her attendants or has arrived there on her own, the innocent girl, seeing me fallen at her feet, says, "Come, rise, my dear, I am not angry," her eyes clouded with tears, her hands trembling from a tight embrace, while being restrained by her friends. (Kok 2.38)
"O fierce one, abandon your anger toward your attendants; it was fate that offended here, by which this great and untimely separation of us two was brought about.

Thus, as she stood before her with hands folded in supplication, her wrath having been appeased, I, becoming one with her, rose up to console her with hundreds of endearments for her beloved. (Kok 2.39)

Seeing her moon-like face, pale and with curls hanging down, reflected upon a wall made of pure crystal, she spoke to her friends in fear, asking, "Who has brought the moon, covered by fragments of clouds, inside the house? Or rather, she spoke thus out of fear.
Having somehow finally fallen asleep there, she remained awake for a long while; alas, she pressed me in a hollow embrace, crushing my breasts as if they were mountains.
She broke her own bracelet held in her hand until only a remnant remained, while watching the lotus-eyes of her friends as they grew heavy with sleep. (Kok 2.41)
The crow announces the arrival of a friend at the southern milk-tree; my left eye throbs, and today at last my heart sighs with relief.
Moreover, the sweet-sounding cry of the cuckoos arises; thus, O brother, somehow maintaining hope for my life, I cling to it.
"Having abandoned him, I live as if equal to the breath of life"—is she ashamed, or is she astonished? Or does she remain here out of hope for reunion with him, for that is the ultimate motive?
Or perhaps she grieves for me, her beloved, who cannot endure separation—such is merely a glimpse of the various gestures of women arising from the pain of parting. (Kok 2.43)

That left arm of hers, which was previously moved from the embrace of my neck for the purpose of sleep at the end of our union— its movement constrained by the knots of passion arising from the intensity of our deep embrace— will now throb when you are near her, having been dragged far away by hostile fate.
At night, your face would not be visible to the speaker in the darkness; during the day, she is distracted by her religious observances until midday.
When the rays of the sun become bearable to the touch, you, taking refuge in a jeweled balcony, should cause her to hear my message while she suffers from the unbearable pain of love.

"Having abandoned even the flowering mango trees, has he come near me perhaps wishing to tell some news of his welfare?"—seeing him with his eyes wiped by your hand which held drops of water, you should begin to speak slowly in clear syllables. (Kok 2.46)
"Unfading and lovely-limbed one, victory be unto you, you who are the auspicious ornament of your husband! I have come from his side as a messenger with a message.
Know me to be born from the lineage of cuckoos whose voices are pleasing to the ear—a sixth weapon of the five-arrowed god that mysteriously captivates travelers. (Kok 2.47)
"O fair-faced one, your beloved dwells among the Cedis and is well; he asks after you, asking whether you enjoy good health.
When you have thus spoken, she—her eyes like wine, her face lit with a smile of joy—will say again and again, "Tell me, tell me," and honor you with sidelong glances mingled with tears.

You should speak thus again: "O you who were born when love and anger arose between you two, and who at that moment became restless with your previous speech—let this very voice of your lord of life, whose love has long been separated from yours, be heard by me; it is sweet to the ear and composed in a pleasing manner. (Kok 2.49)
O lady of auspicious limbs, by means of my external senses, which fail to reach you, my dear companion, I am entering a certain supreme state;
yet this blessed mind, day and night, remains immersed in you regardless of all else—alas, for those born as separate entities, such fortune is indeed singular!
Alas, in every night, as I wallow in the lake called "Agony" while being threatened by the fierce breezes from the lilies that intoxicate the bees,
and while the world sleeps in silence, my companions— the crying, restless-eyed ruddy geese— become my helpers as I am consumed by sighs and anxiety.
Out of delusion he dwells in non-duality; fortitude dissolves, dullness acts like a fish, madness shines forth, and his intellect wanders—such as this I do not know.
Discharging arrows while wandering about, neither sleeping nor eating, the wielder of the five arrows alone knows everything regarding my slow gait. (Kok 2.52)
And at this time, these lovely creepers, laden with blossoming bees and their tips trembling with young shoots, have been kissed by the southern breeze;
they remind me, my beloved, of you as you were during our dalliance—sighing, biting your bud-like lower lip slightly, and shaking your hands.

O slender-limbed one, remembering again and again how you moved about near the jeweled windows at the end of our previous play— your heavy mass of hair hanging loosely over your shoulders and the hem of your garment held by your hand— I can only with great difficulty endure this gentle breeze, which is the kinsman of the fragrance of blooming *bakula* flowers, as I grow faint.
Having somehow crossed the night, which was heavy with separation and intense heat, and seeing the reddish ray of the sun at the edge of the horizon belonging to the enemy of Jambha,
the young man named Cakra— his heart longing for you, O gazelle-eyed one— embraces that woman who hastens toward him to meet him, alas, for the sake of the limit of his fortune.
Longing for you, O beloved, I cast my eyes constantly upon the direction where your mind dwells and where the cry of the charming female swan resounds;
I fix my love upon my own body whenever it is touched by you, and truly, I hold even my very life-breaths as dearer than anything else to you.
"Both you and I have come to this earth"—this thought of non-separation makes us both feel reproached; "remember that," such is the joy of the mutual blending of our words.
"Our limbs are touched simultaneously at night by the rays of the moon"—by that too, there is a true sense of an embrace even during the elephant's gait.
Alas! In this separation from one whose face is so difficult to behold, that very divine creeper of meditation is my sole support.
Having repeatedly and firmly embraced you as you sat upon it out of passion, and having mounted your lap—O lady of heavy hips—it is not fitting to say anything else. (Kok 2.58)
O fair-browed one, the mind of the warrior Madana has today become a worthy target, pierced by many arrows; his fortitude is surely failing.
As his physical form wastes away with time, only his fever does not diminish; indeed, even the flush of color upon his skin increases through the fierce fire of love.
Indeed, there are no means of living in separation from you of such a kind; it is true that I survive by maintaining my fortitude through various [artifices], O Lord of my life.
Having thus resolved, I have desisted from rash acts toward you of incomparable virtue; and you, in turn, should not refuse the requests of your peers regarding bathing and other such matters.
O frail one, by the grace of the Daughter of the Mountain, the ocean of separation is almost crossed; endure the remaining two months and do not despair.
Then, O timid one, we shall sport within the fragrant palace chambers perfumed by rising incense, while the days are made resonant by the thundering of fresh rain-clouds.
O girl with tremulous side-glances, does that face of yours ever flash upon my mind—your face with its white eyes, its Bimba-lip washed clean, and its crest-jewel fallen during the bath?
O friend, while I was gazing at your face as you emerged from your bath, we both suddenly dived once more into the water up to our chests.
O fierce one, seeing some youth there in the pleasure garden embracing various creepers with his vine-like arms around the mango tree,
you turned your face aside and, with your quivering lower lip, sent a sidelong glance toward me— a frown accompanied by droplets of water.
Having been rejected with anger by you when I approached you in love, I was reflected upon your breast; unaware of my presence, the female servant began to cover it with sandalwood paste.
As the circle of friends, filled with smiles, remarked, "Lest she smear more camphor upon this hair-raising spot," you cast a glance at them that was heavy with shame.
While you were gathering garden flowers with your hand, which possessed the luster of young shoots, and while the bees— greedy for the fragrance of my lotus-face—
were clinging to it, your playful companions, as if terrified by the pollen, closed their eyes for a moment even with their sprout-like hands.
Know my well-being from this gift of a token of recognition; furthermore, listen to one more companioning practice of asceticism (*dhūta*):
when the pleasure-swans, possessed by passion, forcibly kiss you while you are slightly moaning, you must look at me with a look of intense bashfulness, remembering something. (Kok 2.66)
The worldly proverb that "passion is broken by separation" applies to me a hundredfold more in your case than in others; for while in union it is one thing, in separation it is quite another.
In union, you are indeed but one; yet in parting, this entire threefold world becomes composed of nothing but you.
Having performed this service for my afflicted brother, O dear friend, may you become the vanguard in the world’s distribution of compassion for those who possess it.
Indeed, they praise you as a cuckoo when, in your childhood, you were reared by others; yet now, O ornament of the assembly of mendicants, you support others through your own maintenance.

Thus, having established her life which is distressed by separation, go now to roam at your pleasure to whatever direction you desire. O honorable one, may you be as dear to the King of Love as the cuckoo is to him; may there never be for you even a single occasion of such separation from her.
